incidents.title: United States military restricts reporters to escorted press pools during the Gulf War
incidents.jurisdiction: United States, federal (military theater: Saudi Arabia and the Persian Gulf)
incidents.summary: The U.S. military required reporters covering the 1991 Gulf War to work in escorted "pools" rather than move freely, reviewed pool dispatches before release, and reporters who left the pools were captured or detained.
incidents.what_happened: During the Gulf War (January to February 1991), the Pentagon, the U.S. Department of Defense, required most journalists covering U.S. forces to join escorted press pools rather than travel independently. Public affairs officers accompanied every pooled reporter, and dispatches passed through a security review before release, officials said, "for its conformance to ... ground rules, not for its potential to express criticism or cause embarrassment." Assistant Secretary of Defense Pete Williams said free movement risked lives; Defense Secretary Dick Cheney said withholding operational detail served the same purpose. Journalists including CBS's Bob Simon left the pool system and were captured by Iraqi forces; others who evaded escorts were arrested by U.S. military police. The Nation and other publications sued the Department of Defense in Nation Magazine v. United States Department of Defense, arguing the pool system violated the First Amendment, the U.S. constitutional guarantee of press freedom.
incidents.stated_justification: Assistant Secretary of Defense Pete Williams said unrestricted reporters risked their own lives and troops' lives; Defense Secretary Dick Cheney said releasing operational detail could help Iraqi forces: "every detail we offer would increase the likelihood that the military forces of Iraq could learn more about our operations."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Reporters could reach the front only through pools with military escorts and pre-release review of dispatches; those who worked outside the system, including a CBS crew, were captured or detained, and coverage relied heavily on Pentagon briefings.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: U.S.-led coalition forces' campaign to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait after Iraq's August 1990 invasion.
incidents.outcome_note: The pool system stayed in place through the war's end on February 28, 1991; the legal challenge in Nation Magazine v. Department of Defense was later dismissed as moot.

incidents.title: Pentagon sets ground rules for journalists embedded with United States forces in Iraq
incidents.summary: Ahead of the 2003 invasion of Iraq, the Pentagon assigned about 600 journalists to travel with United States military units under written ground rules restricting what they could report about troop numbers, operations and casualties.
incidents.what_happened: In February 2003, before the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Pentagon, the U.S. Department of Defense, issued written ground rules for reporters embedded with military units. The rules barred disclosing specific troop numbers below corps level, future operations, rules of engagement and identifying details of casualties or captured enemy prisoners for 72 hours or until families were notified. The Pentagon said the limits were meant "for the safety and security of U.S. forces and embedded media" and were "in no way intended to prevent release of derogatory, embarrassing, negative or uncomplimentary information." About 600 journalists joined the program, travelling with units through the invasion that began March 20, 2003. Embargoes on operational details were to lift once the security concern passed. Critics said access depended on units' cooperation and that embedded reporters saw only a narrow slice of the war; supporters said embedding produced far more front-line coverage than the restricted pools of the 1991 Gulf War.
incidents.stated_justification: The Pentagon said the ground rules existed "for the safety and security of U.S. forces and embedded media" and were "in no way intended to prevent release of derogatory, embarrassing, negative or uncomplimentary information."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Embedded reporters gained sustained front-line access in exchange for accepting restrictions on troop numbers, future operations and casualty details, and for accepting embargoes lifted only once the military judged the security concern had passed.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The buildup to and launch of the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in March 2003.
incidents.outcome_note: The embedding program ran through the invasion and became the Pentagon's standard model for media access in later conflicts.

incidents.title: New York Times reporter Judith Miller jailed for refusing to name a confidential source in the Valerie Plame affair
incidents.summary: A federal judge jailed New York Times reporter Judith Miller for contempt after she refused to tell a grand jury who told her the identity of CIA officer Valerie Plame, part of a special counsel's investigation into the leak.
incidents.what_happened: In 2003, columnist Robert Novak published the name of Valerie Plame, an undercover Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer, after officials in President George W. Bush's administration discussed her identity with reporters after her husband publicly criticized the Iraq War. Special counsel Patrick Fitzgerald investigated the leak and subpoenaed several reporters, including Judith Miller of The New York Times, to testify before a federal grand jury, a panel that decides whether to bring criminal charges. Miller had not published a story about Plame but had discussed her with a source, Vice President Dick Cheney's chief of staff I. Lewis "Scooter" Libby, and refused to identify him, citing a reporter's duty to protect sources. On July 6, 2005, federal judge Thomas F. Hogan found her in civil contempt and jailed her. She was released on September 29, 2005, after Libby released her from confidentiality and she agreed to testify. Libby was later convicted of perjury and obstruction.
incidents.stated_justification: Judge Hogan held that Miller's refusal to identify her source obstructed a federal grand jury investigation into a possible crime; Miller said, "If journalists cannot be trusted to keep confidences, then journalists cannot function and there cannot be a free press."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Miller spent 85 days in jail for declining to reveal a source for a story she never wrote, a rare instance of a United States reporter jailed over source confidentiality, and other reporters subpoenaed in the same case negotiated releases from their sources instead.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Bush administration's case for the 2003 Iraq War and the public dispute over former ambassador Joseph Wilson's contrary account of Iraqi uranium claims.
incidents.outcome_note: Courts upheld the contempt order and subpoena; Miller served 85 days before her source freed her to testify, and prosecutors later convicted Libby of perjury.

incidents.title: United States charges Army analyst Chelsea Manning under the Espionage Act for leaking to WikiLeaks
incidents.summary: The U.S. Army charged intelligence analyst Chelsea Manning under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, after she gave WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents, a large archive of military and diplomatic files that news organizations later published.
incidents.what_happened: In 2010, U.S. Army intelligence analyst Chelsea Manning gave WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents, a large archive of military reports and diplomatic cables, including video of a 2007 helicopter strike in Baghdad. The material included, the American Civil Liberties Union said, "evidence of civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan, U.S. attempts to cover up the CIA torture program, and other matters of public interest." WikiLeaks and news partners including The Guardian and The New York Times published selections. The Army charged Manning under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, and, more unusually, with "aiding the enemy," a capital military offense; prosecutors did not allege she gave material directly to any adversary. A military court convicted her in 2013 on Espionage Act counts but acquitted her of aiding the enemy, and sentenced her to 35 years, the longest sentence given a leaker in United States history. President Obama commuted the sentence in January 2017.
incidents.stated_justification: Military prosecutors said Manning's disclosures endangered lives and national security; the ACLU said the "aiding the enemy" charge was "akin to treason and punishable by death" despite no allegation she gave material to an adversary directly.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The prosecution set a United States record for a leak sentence and became a reference point for later Espionage Act cases against sources for journalists; the ACLU said, "When a soldier who shared information with the press and public is punished far more harshly than others who tortured prisoners and killed civilians, something is seriously wrong with our justice system."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: United States conduct of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and detainee treatment, including the CIA's interrogation program.
incidents.outcome_note: Manning's convictions were not overturned, but President Obama commuted her 35-year sentence in January 2017 and she was released that May.

incidents.title: United States prosecutes former CIA officer John Kiriakou under the Espionage Act for identifying a covert colleague to a journalist
incidents.summary: Former CIA officer John Kiriakou, who in 2007 was the first CIA officer to publicly describe the agency's waterboarding of a detainee, pleaded guilty to identifying a covert colleague to a journalist and was sentenced under the Espionage Act to 30 months in prison.
incidents.what_happened: John Kiriakou, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer, said publicly in a 2007 television interview that the CIA had waterboarded a detainee, the first time an agency officer had confirmed the practice, which international bodies have called torture. Federal prosecutors later charged Kiriakou under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, for identifying a covert CIA officer to a freelance journalist investigating the interrogation program; the journalist did not publish the name. Kiriakou pleaded guilty in October 2012 to one count of passing information to a person not authorized to receive it. U.S. Attorney Neil MacBride said Kiriakou "put the life of a covert officer at risk." On January 25, 2013, Judge Leonie Brinkema sentenced him to 30 months, the statutory minimum under his plea agreement, saying she "wished she could have imposed a greater sentence." No CIA official involved in the interrogation program was prosecuted.
incidents.stated_justification: U.S. Attorney Neil MacBride said, "John Kiriakou put the life of a covert officer at risk; he put the officer's family in danger; and he exposed our nation's vital secrets." Prosecutors also said Kiriakou was motivated by "fame and money."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Kiriakou, not the journalist he spoke with, was prosecuted and imprisoned; press-freedom advocates said the case showed sources faced Espionage Act prosecution for contact with reporters even when no story identifying the covert officer was published.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Public disclosure of the CIA's post-September 11 interrogation program, including its use of waterboarding.
incidents.outcome_note: Kiriakou served his full 30-month sentence under the plea agreement and was released in February 2015; no CIA interrogation-program official faced comparable charges.

incidents.title: United States Justice Department secretly seizes two months of Associated Press phone records
incidents.summary: The U.S. Justice Department secretly obtained two months of telephone records from more than 20 Associated Press phone lines during a leak investigation, notifying the news agency only after the fact; AP called the scope of the seizure unjustified.
incidents.what_happened: In April and May 2012, the Associated Press (AP) reported that the CIA had disrupted a plot by an al-Qaeda affiliate in Yemen to bomb a U.S.-bound airplane. The Justice Department, investigating who disclosed the classified operation, obtained telephone toll records covering more than 20 AP office and staff phone lines in New York, Washington and Hartford, Connecticut, and the AP's line in the U.S. House of Representatives press gallery, without first asking AP for the records, as its own guidelines generally required. AP learned of the seizure when the Justice Department notified it on May 10, 2013, and disclosed it publicly on May 13. AP President Gary Pruitt said, "There can be no possible justification for such an over-broad collection of the telephone communications of The Associated Press and its reporters." More than 100 journalists worked in the offices whose numbers were collected. No journalist or source was ever charged in the underlying leak case.
incidents.stated_justification: Attorney General Eric Holder called the underlying disclosure "among, if not the most serious ... a ... very, very serious leak," and the Justice Department said, "We take seriously our obligations to follow all applicable laws, federal regulations, and Department of Justice policies when issuing subpoenas for phone records of media organisations."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The seizure covered work and personal numbers for AP staff across three bureaus and swept in more than 100 journalists' shared office lines, exposing AP's contacts and sourcing patterns on a wide range of unrelated stories, not only the leak under investigation.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: A May 2012 AP report on a foiled al-Qaeda bomb plot aimed at a U.S.-bound airplane, which the government said compromised an intelligence source.
incidents.outcome_note: The records were not returned and no journalist or source was charged; the Justice Department issued revised media-subpoena guidelines on July 12, 2013, after the disclosure.

incidents.title: United States search warrant names Fox News reporter James Rosen a possible co-conspirator in a leak case
incidents.summary: A 2010 FBI search-warrant affidavit, unsealed in 2013, described Fox News reporter James Rosen as a possible co-conspirator in violating the Espionage Act because he sought classified information from a State Department analyst, and used that theory to obtain his private emails.
incidents.what_happened: In 2009, Fox News reporter James Rosen published a story, based on a State Department analyst's account, that North Korea would likely respond to United Nations sanctions with more nuclear tests. Investigating the leak, an FBI agent wrote in a 2010 warrant affidavit, unsealed and reported in 2013, that Rosen, "in his newsgathering, was violating federal statutes that prohibit 'unauthorized disclosure of national defense information' as an 'aider, abettor, and/or co-conspirator,'" under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information. A federal magistrate approved the warrant, which the Justice Department used to obtain two days of Rosen's personal emails, his phone records and records of his security-badge movements inside the State Department. The analyst, Stephen Kim, was separately charged and later pleaded guilty. Rosen himself was never charged; press-freedom groups said naming a reporter as a criminal co-conspirator for ordinary newsgathering, asking questions and cultivating a source, had no precedent in a warrant against a working journalist.
incidents.stated_justification: The FBI affidavit argued Rosen's newsgathering itself, soliciting classified information and cultivating a source, made him a likely "aider, abettor, and/or co-conspirator" in violating the Espionage Act, the legal theory the Justice Department used to justify seizing his records.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The Justice Department seized Rosen's personal emails, phone records and State Department security-badge logs; the Committee to Protect Journalists said such tactics against reporters had "a chilling effect domestically and sends a terrible message to journalists around the world."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: A 2009 Fox News report, sourced to a State Department analyst, forecasting North Korea's response to new United Nations sanctions.
incidents.outcome_note: The warrant was not withdrawn from the record; Kim pleaded guilty in 2014 and Rosen was never charged. Holder's July 2013 guidelines later restricted subpoenas naming reporters as suspects.

incidents.title: United States pursues New York Times reporter James Risen's testimony for years before dropping its demand for his source
incidents.summary: For years, federal prosecutors sought New York Times reporter James Risen's testimony identifying a confidential source in a CIA leak case; the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal, but Attorney General Eric Holder ultimately chose not to force him to testify or name the source.
incidents.what_happened: James Risen, a reporter for The New York Times, wrote in a 2006 book and in earlier newspaper articles about a botched CIA operation aimed at Iran's nuclear program, citing an unnamed source. Federal prosecutors identified former CIA officer Jeffrey Sterling as a suspect and, starting in 2008, subpoenaed Risen to testify before a grand jury and later at Sterling's trial, seeking to make him confirm Sterling was his source. Risen refused and fought the subpoena through the courts; the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in 2013 that reporters had no First Amendment privilege to withhold a source's identity in a criminal case, and the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in 2014. Attorney General Eric Holder then approved only a limited subpoena that did not ask Risen to identify his source, and in October 2014 said prosecutors would not force him to testify at all. Sterling was convicted in January 2015 using other evidence, without Risen's testimony.
incidents.stated_justification: Prosecutors said Risen's direct testimony was necessary to prove Sterling was his source; Attorney General Eric Holder said of the resolution, "the way in which that case was handled after the new policies were put in place [is] an example of how the Justice Department can proceed."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Risen faced years of legal jeopardy, including the threat of jail for contempt, before prosecutors relented; the case became a benchmark for how far the government would press reporters to identify sources in national-security leak prosecutions.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: A 2006 book account of a botched CIA operation meant to disrupt Iran's nuclear weapons program.
incidents.outcome_note: After the Supreme Court declined to hear Risen's appeal, the Justice Department chose not to compel his testimony or the identity of his source; Sterling was convicted without it.

incidents.title: White House revokes CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credential after a news conference exchange with President Trump
incidents.summary: After CNN's Jim Acosta questioned President Trump at a news conference and briefly kept hold of a microphone as an intern reached for it, the White House suspended his hard pass, the standing credential letting reporters enter the grounds; a federal judge ordered it restored a week later.
incidents.what_happened: At a November 7, 2018 White House news conference, President Trump and CNN correspondent Jim Acosta argued over Acosta's questions about immigration; when a White House intern reached to take his microphone, Acosta held onto it and briefly touched her arm. That evening, Press Secretary Sarah Sanders announced the suspension of Acosta's hard pass, the standing credential letting reporters enter the White House grounds, saying the White House would "never tolerate a reporter placing his hands on a young woman just trying to do her job." CNN called the suspension "a threat to our democracy" and sued the White House on November 13, arguing the revocation violated the First Amendment, the constitutional guarantee of press freedom, and the Fifth Amendment's guarantee of due process. On November 16, federal judge Timothy Kelly ordered the pass restored while the case proceeded; Acosta told reporters, "Let's go back to work." The White House restored the pass permanently on November 19 rather than continue the litigation.
incidents.stated_justification: Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said, "We will, however, never tolerate a reporter placing his hands on a young woman just trying to do her job as a White House intern." Government lawyers separately argued Acosta had no First Amendment right of access to the White House.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: CNN said the revocation was "a threat to our democracy," and other outlets, including some critical of Acosta's conduct, joined an emergency court filing warning that a president could use credential revocation to penalize unfavorable questioning.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: President Trump's characterization of a migrant caravan approaching the United States border in the days before the November 2018 midterm election.
incidents.outcome_note: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on November 16, 2018, and the White House permanently restored Acosta's credential three days later rather than continue the lawsuit.

incidents.title: United States indicts WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange under the Espionage Act
incidents.summary: The United States indicted WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange on 17 counts under the Espionage Act over the 2010 publication of leaked military and diplomatic files, charges press-freedom groups said could expose ordinary national-security journalism to prosecution.
incidents.what_happened: On May 23, 2019, the U.S. Justice Department added 17 counts under the Espionage Act, a 1917 law against disclosing defense information, to an existing charge against Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents. The new counts concerned WikiLeaks' 2010 publication of classified military reports and diplomatic cables supplied by U.S. Army analyst Chelsea Manning. Assistant Attorney General John Demers said, "Julian Assange is no journalist," and the department said his actions "risked serious harm to United States national security to the benefit of our adversaries." Assange's attorney, Barry Pollack, said the charges "demonstrate the gravity of the threat the criminal prosecution of Julian Assange poses to all journalists," since the conduct charged, receiving and publishing classified material from a source, is conduct news organizations routinely engage in. Assange was then in British custody after his April 2019 arrest at Ecuador's London embassy; the United States sought his extradition.
incidents.stated_justification: Assistant Attorney General John Demers said, "Julian Assange is no journalist, this is made plain by the totality of his conduct as alleged in the indictment," and the department said his actions "risked serious harm to United States national security to the benefit of our adversaries."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Assange's attorney and press-freedom groups said charging the receipt and publication of leaked classified material under the Espionage Act, rather than only its unauthorized disclosure, could expose ordinary national-security journalism to prosecution.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: WikiLeaks' 2010 publication of leaked United States military reports and diplomatic cables supplied by Chelsea Manning.
incidents.outcome_note: Assange spent five years in a British prison fighting extradition before a June 2024 plea deal: he pleaded guilty to one count, was sentenced to time served, and was released.

incidents.title: Turkey closes more than 100 media outlets by decree after a failed coup attempt
incidents.summary: After a failed July 2016 coup attempt, Turkey's government closed more than 100 newspapers, television and radio stations, news agencies and publishing houses by state-of-emergency decree, citing alleged links to the movement it blamed for the coup.
incidents.what_happened: On July 15, 2016, a faction of Turkey's military attempted to seize power; the government put down the attempt within hours. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government declared a state of emergency on July 21, giving it power to rule by decree, an executive order with the force of law that bypasses ordinary parliamentary debate. Decree No. 668, issued July 27, 2016, closed 131 media outlets, including 45 newspapers, 16 television channels, three news agencies, 23 radio stations, 15 magazines and 29 publishing houses, all accused of having "links to a terrorist organization" and posing "a threat to national security." The government said the outlets had ties to the movement of the US-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom it accused of directing the coup attempt. Further decrees followed, including a September 28 order closing stations popular among Kurdish and Alevi audiences and opposition supporters; by December 2016, 140 outlets and 29 publishers had been shut. Human Rights Watch said the closures extended well beyond outlets with any documented Gulen movement connection.
incidents.stated_justification: The government said the closed outlets had "links to a terrorist organization" and posed "a threat to national security," tying them to the movement of U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom it accused of directing the coup attempt.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: More than 100 newspapers, broadcasters, news agencies and publishing houses lost their operating licenses at a stroke, and Reporters Without Borders said the decrees eliminated "an entire swathe" of Turkey's media in one action.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The failed July 15, 2016 coup attempt against President Erdogan's government and the mass arrests and dismissals that followed against alleged participants and sympathizers.

incidents.title: Nigeria's military government convicts journalists by special tribunal over coup-plot reporting
incidents.summary: A special military tribunal convicted four Nigerian journalists as accessories to a supposed 1995 coup plot after they reported on it, sentencing them to lengthy prison terms with no right of appeal, under the military government of General Sani Abacha.
incidents.what_happened: In March 1995, Nigeria's military government, led by General Sani Abacha, announced it had uncovered a coup plot and arrested dozens of soldiers and civilians, including former head of state Olusegun Obasanjo. Journalists Kunle Ajibade, Chris Anyanwu, George Mbah and Ben Charles-Obi had reported on the alleged plot; the government said their reporting exposed security information and cast doubt on the coup allegation. A Special Military Tribunal, a panel of military officers with no requirement to observe ordinary court procedure or allow appeal, tried the journalists alongside the alleged plotters and convicted them as "accessories after the fact to treason." Ajibade received a life sentence, later commuted to 15 years; Anyanwu received 15 years; Mbah and Charles-Obi received 15 years each. One tribunal official said the prosecutions were meant "to deter others from the irresponsibilities of Nigerian journalism." The Committee to Protect Journalists said the case was part of a broader campaign using indefinite detention, secret military trials and violence against Nigeria's independent press.
incidents.stated_justification: A security official told one journalist the story "had caused some security problems and discredited the government's coup allegation"; a tribunal official said the prosecutions were meant "to deter others from the irresponsibilities of Nigerian journalism."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Four journalists received prison terms of up to 15 years with no right of appeal for reporting on a coup allegation the government itself had announced, part of what CPJ called "a calculated, and almost successful, campaign to decimate" Nigeria's independent press.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: An alleged March 1995 coup plot against General Sani Abacha's military government, which the journalists had reported on.
incidents.outcome_note: The journalists were released in stages after General Abacha's death in June 1998 under his successor's government; their convictions were not vacated in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: Malaysia pressures domestic media and monitors foreign correspondents after arresting former deputy premier Anwar Ibrahim
incidents.summary: After Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's government arrested former deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim in September 1998, party-linked newspapers pressured staff to follow the official line, police visited journalists who interviewed his wife, and authorities said they would monitor internet traffic about the case.
incidents.what_happened: On September 20, 1998, Malaysian police arrested former deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, days after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad dismissed him amid a political dispute; Anwar was later convicted on corruption and sodomy charges he said were fabricated to end his political career. Newspapers partly owned by the ruling United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), including Utusan Malaysia, pressured editors and journalists to follow the party line on the case or face dismissal, Human Rights Watch reported. Police visited foreign correspondents in Singapore who had interviewed Anwar's wife, Wan Azizah, as part of a sedition investigation into her, and authorities barred her from addressing public meetings. incidents.title: State-controlled Gazprom takes formal control of Russia's independent NTV television network
incidents.summary: Gazprom, Russia's state-controlled gas company, used debts owed by NTV's parent company to take control of the country's last major independent television network at a shareholders' meeting, replacing its owner and top editors with its own appointees.
incidents.what_happened: NTV, founded by media entrepreneur Vladimir Gusinsky, was Russia's most-watched independent television network and had criticized the government's conduct of the war in Chechnya. Gazprom, Russia's state-controlled gas company, had extended loans to Gusinsky's holding company, Media-Most, and after Gusinsky left Russia facing separate criminal proceedings, Gazprom called in the debt and obtained enough shares to control NTV. On April 14, 2001, Gazprom-Media used a shareholders' meeting to take formal control, removing Gusinsky and managing director Yevgeny Kiselyov from the board and installing Alfred Kokh as chairman and Boris Jordan as general director. NTV staff said in a statement, "We realize that the ultimate goal of this meeting ... is establishing full control over our company." Gusinsky and Kiselyov said the takeover was a Kremlin-directed effort to end independent national television under President Vladimir Putin. The Committee to Protect Journalists said it was "very concerned about Gazprom-Media's potential interference in the editorial decisions of NTV journalists."
incidents.stated_justification: Gazprom framed the takeover as debt collection from Gusinsky's Media-Most holding company; Gusinsky and Kiselyov said it was, in substance, "a Kremlin-directed campaign to rein in Russia's only remaining independent national TV station."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: NTV's founder and top editorial leadership were removed and replaced with Gazprom appointees; CPJ said it remained "very concerned about Gazprom-Media's potential interference in the editorial decisions of NTV journalists" going forward.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: NTV's critical coverage of Russia's second war in Chechnya and of the government of President Vladimir Putin, who had taken office in May 2000.
incidents.outcome_note: The takeover was not reversed; most of NTV's original staff resigned in the following weeks rather than work under the new management.

incidents.title: Zimbabwe enacts a law requiring all journalists and media houses to hold government licenses
incidents.summary: Zimbabwe's parliament passed the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA), requiring every journalist and media company to obtain a government license renewed every two years, weeks before a closely contested 2002 presidential election.
incidents.what_happened: In March 2002, weeks before a presidential election, Zimbabwe's government, led by President Robert Mugabe, enacted the Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA). The law required every journalist and media company to be licensed by a government-appointed regulator, the Media and Information Commission, with licenses renewable every two years, and created new offenses for publishing information officials deemed false. Freedom House said the law "requires all journalists and media companies to be licensed, imposes strict content restrictions, and grants broad powers to a government-controlled regulator." Independent outlets and press-freedom groups opposed the law in principle, saying statutory licensing of print media had no place in a democracy; some foreign correspondents were denied accreditation and independent papers, including the Daily News, were later prosecuted for operating without a license. A 2007 amendment eased individual accreditation requirements outside covering Parliament or official events, but Freedom House said the framework remained "extremely restrictive."
incidents.stated_justification: The law's licensing and content provisions were presented as regulating professional standards and accountability in the media; the sources reviewed did not record a specific quoted government defense beyond the law's own grant of power to a state-appointed regulator.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Every journalist and media house needed a government-issued, renewable license to operate; independent outlets that published without one, including the Daily News, faced closure, and Freedom House called the framework "extremely restrictive, with onerous licensing requirements."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Zimbabwe's contested March 2002 presidential election, in which President Mugabe faced international criticism over the vote's conduct.
incidents.outcome_note: The record reviewed documents a 2007 amendment easing individual accreditation but does not establish to day precision when AIPPA's licensing framework was repealed.

incidents.title: Investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya is shot dead in Moscow; a former police officer is later convicted of organizing the killing
incidents.summary: Anna Politkovskaya, a Novaya Gazeta journalist known for reporting critical of Russia's conduct of the war in Chechnya, was shot dead in her Moscow apartment building; a Moscow court later convicted a former police officer of organizing surveillance for her killers.
incidents.what_happened: Anna Politkovskaya, a reporter for the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was known for reporting on human-rights abuses during Russia's war in Chechnya, a mostly Muslim region in Russia's North Caucasus, and for criticism of President Vladimir Putin's government. On October 7, 2006, Putin's birthday, she was shot dead in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building. Investigators eventually charged several men, including Sergei Khadzhikurbanov, reported as a former police officer, and, later, Dmitry Pavlyuchenkov, a former officer in a Moscow police surveillance unit, who pleaded guilty in 2012 to tracking Politkovskaya's movements and supplying the gun used to kill her. A Moscow court sentenced Pavlyuchenkov to 11 years in exchange for his cooperation; he told the court, "I want to appeal to the family of Anna Stepanovna; I simply want to ask for their human forgiveness." Five men were eventually convicted; who ordered the killing was never conclusively established in court. The Kremlin did not immediately comment on her death.
incidents.stated_justification: No government body said it was responsible or offered a public justification; investigators built their case around the men convicted of organizing and carrying out the killing, including a former police surveillance officer, without conclusively naming who ordered it.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The Russian Union of Journalists' Igor Yakovenko called it "clearly a contract killing," and the International Federation of Journalists said it "reflects on the state of lawlessness that is threatening to overwhelm the whole of Russian journalism."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Politkovskaya's investigative reporting on human-rights abuses in Chechnya and her criticism of the Russian government's conduct there.
incidents.outcome_note: Courts convicted and sentenced five men, including former police officer Dmitry Pavlyuchenkov, for organizing or carrying out the killing; who ordered it was never conclusively established in court.

incidents.title: Iran expels a BBC correspondent and restricts foreign journalists after a disputed 2009 election

The government revoked accreditation for many foreign journalists, barred them from reporting from the streets, and permitted only phone interviews and official government sources; Al Arabiya's Tehran operation was temporarily suspended. Foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki called the election "a very transparent competition" and accused Britain of interference without providing evidence. Authorities also blocked numerous websites and limited mobile-phone text messaging during the unrest that followed.

incidents.effect_on_reporting: Foreign correspondents lost accreditation and were confined largely to phone interviews and official sources rather than street reporting; one report said the government revoked all foreign press passes during the unrest, forcing some journalists to work without official credentials.

incidents.title: Hungary's parliament gives a government-appointed media council power to fine outlets for unbalanced coverage
incidents.summary: Hungary's parliament, controlled by Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party, passed a media law creating a government-appointed National Media and Infocommunications Authority empowered to fine any outlet, print, broadcast or online, for coverage it deemed unbalanced or offensive to public morality.
incidents.what_happened: In December 2010, Hungary's parliament, where Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party held a two-thirds majority, passed a media law creating the National Media and Infocommunications Authority, a regulator whose board is appointed by the parliamentary majority for nine-year terms. The law let the authority impose fines, reported at up to roughly half a million dollars per violation, on any news outlet it judged had produced "unbalanced" coverage or violated vaguely defined standards of "public morality," and required outlets to register with the state. The law took effect January 1, 2011. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe called the media council's power "unprecedented in European democracies," and former European Union Commissioner Laszlo Kovacs said, "The law provides total control to the government over all the media, both public and private." Orban said the government was "monitoring its practical application" and would address concerns if verified; a Media Council legal official acknowledged the country's earlier "unfettered press freedom" had also produced problems.
incidents.stated_justification: Prime Minister Orban said the government was "monitoring its practical application and if any of the political concerns are verified ... we are ready to remedy them," while a Media Council legal official said Hungary's earlier "unfettered press freedom" had "yielded some negative fruit as well."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Every news outlet, print, broadcast or online, became subject to fines of up to roughly half a million dollars for coverage a government-appointed board deemed unbalanced; the OSCE called the board's power "unprecedented in European democracies."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The incoming Fidesz government's broader effort, after its April 2010 election win, to restructure Hungary's state institutions, including media regulation.
incidents.outcome_note: The law took effect January 1, 2011, and, after European Union criticism, Hungary amended some provisions in 2011 but kept the media authority's core licensing and fining powers.

incidents.title: Ecuador's Organic Communication Law creates a regulator that issues hundreds of sanctions against journalists and outlets
incidents.summary: Ecuador's National Assembly passed the Organic Communication Law under President Rafael Correa, creating the Superintendency of Information and Communication (SUPERCOM), a regulator that issued more than 675 sanctions against journalists and media outlets over the following four years.
incidents.what_happened: On June 25, 2013, Ecuador's National Assembly, controlled by allies of President Rafael Correa, passed the Organic Communication Law, which created the Superintendency of Information and Communication (SUPERCOM), a regulator empowered to fine, reprimand or order public apologies from journalists and outlets found to have violated the law's content rules, provisions the United Nations and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights said were used against coverage unfavorable to the government. Within four years, SUPERCOM had opened 1,081 cases and issued 675 sanctions, by its own count, split by the monitoring group Fundamedios into 324 fines, 137 written reprimands and 54 forced public apologies. SUPERCOM itself said the law guaranteed rather than restricted press freedom because "in four years no media outlet has been closed." After Correa left office, President Lenin Moreno proposed eliminating SUPERCOM in 2018; his communications secretary said, "If we're in a constructive process, we should get rid of the Supercom."

incidents.effect_on_reporting: SUPERCOM opened 1,081 cases and issued 675 sanctions against journalists and outlets in four years, including fines, written reprimands and forced public apologies, a pattern Fundamedios and international monitors said pressured critical coverage.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: President Correa's long-running public disputes with Ecuadorian media over their coverage of his government, including a separate 2011 libel case against the newspaper El Universo.
incidents.outcome_note: President Lenin Moreno's government moved to eliminate SUPERCOM in 2018; Fundamedios director Cesar Ricaurte said the surrounding legal framework nonetheless remained "intact."

incidents.title: Egypt arrests and later convicts three Al Jazeera journalists on terrorism-related charges
incidents.summary: Months after the military removed President Mohamed Morsi, Egyptian security forces arrested Al Jazeera English journalists Peter Greste, Mohamed Fahmy and Baher Mohamed at a Cairo hotel; courts later convicted them of aiding a banned organization, and international pressure led to pardons.
incidents.what_happened: On December 29, 2013, Egyptian security forces arrested Al Jazeera English correspondent Peter Greste, bureau chief Mohamed Fahmy and producer Baher Mohamed at Cairo's Marriott Hotel, months after the military, led by then-Defense Minister Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, removed elected President Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood, which the government later designated a terrorist organization. Al Jazeera called the verdict "a deliberate attack on press freedom"; Greste, already deported and tried in absentia, said, "We did nothing wrong. The court presented no evidence." President Sisi pardoned Fahmy and Mohamed on September 23, 2015, as part of a wider amnesty.

incidents.title: Poland's new government gains power to replace public broadcaster leadership, and journalists are dismissed
incidents.summary: Weeks after winning power, Poland's Law and Justice (PiS) party passed a law letting the treasury minister directly appoint and dismiss the heads of public radio and television, and dozens of journalists at the public broadcaster were subsequently dismissed or resigned.
incidents.what_happened: Poland's Law and Justice (PiS) party won parliamentary and presidential elections in 2015 and, within weeks of taking office, passed a "small" media law, signed by President Andrzej Duda on December 31, 2015, giving the treasury minister power to appoint and dismiss the heads of public radio and television broadcasters directly, without the previously required independent broadcasting council process. Reporters Without Borders said the law "gave the ruling party close control of the public media." Under Prime Minister Beata Szydlo's government, dozens of journalists and executives at the public broadcasters TVP and Polish Radio were dismissed or resigned in the following months, part of what one former colleague called a "political cleansing" that began at the top and moved through the ranks, affecting first "journalists and editors of news and current affairs programmes." RSF said firing "experienced journalists whose professionalism has never been disputed violates a democratic society's rules and threatens press freedom," and that the changes "helped precipitate Poland's rapid fall" in its press-freedom rankings.
incidents.stated_justification: The government did not offer an individualized public justification for each dismissal in the sources reviewed; a former colleague of those removed described management as seeking staff viewed as ideologically reliable rather than only professionally qualified.

incidents.title: Cambodia's government forces the closure of The Cambodia Daily with a disputed multimillion-dollar tax bill
incidents.summary: Cambodia's tax authority presented the independent, English-language Cambodia Daily with a $6.3 million bill the paper called arbitrary and undocumented, forcing the 24-year-old newspaper to close rather than pay, amid a wider campaign against independent media before 2018 elections.
incidents.what_happened: The Cambodia Daily, an independent English-language newspaper covering Cambodian politics and human rights since 1993, was presented by the tax authority with a $6.3 million bill covering several years of alleged unpaid taxes. The paper said the figure was "arbitrary" and not based on any audit of its books, and Prime Minister Hun Sen, in a speech, called the paper's owners "thieves" and said, of their response, "When they didn't pay and we asked them to leave the country, they said we are a dictatorship." Unable to pay or successfully dispute the bill by the government's deadline, the paper published its final edition on September 4, 2017, headlined "Descent Into Outright Dictatorship," and closed after 24 years. Human Rights Watch's Phil Robertson called the closure "one of the gravest threats to freedom of the press in Cambodia since the 1991 Paris Peace Accords." The closure came amid a wider campaign against independent media and civil-society groups ahead of Cambodia's 2018 elections, which Hun Sen's party went on to win after the main opposition party was dissolved by court order.
incidents.stated_justification: The tax department presented the $6.3 million bill as owed back taxes; the newspaper said the figure was "arbitrary" and not based on an audit, and Prime Minister Hun Sen said of the dispute, "When they didn't pay and we asked them to leave the country, they said we are a dictatorship."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: An independent newspaper that had covered Cambodian politics and rights issues for 24 years closed rather than pay a bill it could not verify; Human Rights Watch called it "one of the gravest threats to freedom of the press in Cambodia since the 1991 Paris Peace Accords."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Preparations for Cambodia's 2018 general election and a wider government campaign against independent media and civil-society groups seen as sympathetic to the opposition.
incidents.outcome_note: The Cambodia Daily did not reopen; its closure coincided with a wider campaign against independent outlets and civil-society groups ahead of Cambodia's 2018 election.

incidents.title: Tanzania requires bloggers and online publishers to register and pay an annual government fee
incidents.summary: Tanzania's government, under President John Magufuli, issued regulations requiring anyone running a blog or website with user content to register with the telecoms regulator and pay an annual fee reported at roughly $930, with vaguely worded content bans.
incidents.what_happened: On March 16, 2018, Tanzania's government issued the Electronic and Postal Communications (Online Content) Regulations, requiring bloggers, online publishers and operators of websites with user-generated content to register with the Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority (TCRA) and pay a licensing fee reported at roughly $930 a year, a large sum in a country where average annual income is a small fraction of that. The regulations banned vaguely defined categories of content, including material causing "annoyance" or leading to "public disorder," and let the TCRA order content removed without judicial process. The advocacy group ARTICLE 19 said the TCRA "is not independent and giving the body the power to determine illegal content and order its removal lacks due process guarantees." Local media reported officials said the fee was meant to curb "moral decadence" online. Six human-rights and media groups challenged the fee in court and won an injunction in April 2018 while the case proceeded.
incidents.stated_justification: Officials said the regulations were meant to curb what local reporting described as "moral decadence" online and to make bloggers and online publishers accountable in the way licensed broadcasters already were.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Anyone running a blog or user-content website had to register and pay roughly $930 a year, a large sum locally, or risk prosecution; ARTICLE 19 said the regulator enforcing the rule "is not independent" and lacked "due process guarantees" for content takedowns.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: A broader push under President Magufuli's government to regulate online speech and civic activity ahead of Tanzania's 2020 general election cycle.
incidents.outcome_note: A court granted media and rights groups an injunction against the fee in April 2018 while their challenge proceeded; the sources reviewed do not establish the challenge's final outcome.

incidents.title: Myanmar sentences two Reuters journalists to seven years under the Official Secrets Act for reporting on a massacre
incidents.summary: A Myanmar court sentenced Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo to seven years under the colonial-era Official Secrets Act after police handed them classified documents at a dinner shortly before their arrest, while they were investigating the killing of Rohingya Muslim villagers.
incidents.what_happened: Reuters reporters Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo were investigating the killing of ten Rohingya Muslim men and boys by soldiers and villagers in Rakhine State when police, in December 2017, invited them to dinner and handed them rolled-up documents just before officers arrested them for possessing the papers. Prosecutors charged them under Myanmar's Official Secrets Act, a colonial-era law against handling state documents without authorization. On September 3, 2018, a judge convicted and sentenced both men to seven years in prison. Reuters editor-in-chief Stephen Adler called it "a sad day for Myanmar, Reuters journalists Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo, and the press everywhere." Human Rights Watch's Brad Adams said, "7 years for reporting the truth is what we expect from dictatorships," and Britain's ambassador said the case "struck a hammer blow to the rule of law." Aung San Suu Kyi's government, in which she held the position of State Counsellor, a de facto head-of-government role created for her since the constitution barred her from the presidency, did not intervene.
incidents.stated_justification: Prosecutors charged the two reporters under the colonial-era Official Secrets Act for possessing documents a police officer had handed them at a dinner shortly before their arrest, a setup the reporters' defense argued at trial.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Two working journalists received seven-year prison sentences for reporting on a documented mass killing; Human Rights Watch's Brad Adams said, "7 years for reporting the truth is what we expect from dictatorships," and the case drew wide international condemnation.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Reuters investigation into the killing of ten Rohingya Muslim men and boys by Myanmar soldiers and local residents in Inn Din village, Rakhine State, in September 2017.
incidents.outcome_note: President Win Myint pardoned and released Wa Lone and Kyaw Soe Oo on May 7, 2019, after 511 days in prison, as part of a mass amnesty.

incidents.title: India imposes a communications blackout in Jammu and Kashmir after revoking the region's special status
incidents.summary: As it revoked Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional autonomy, India's government cut broadband, mobile internet, text messaging and phone service across the region, leaving local journalists unable to file stories, verify information or communicate with sources for months.
incidents.what_happened: On August 5, 2019, India's government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, revoked Article 370 of the Indian constitution, which had granted the Muslim-majority region of Jammu and Kashmir a degree of autonomy, and split it into two federally administered territories. Ahead of the announcement, authorities cut broadband, mobile internet, text messaging and phone service across the region and detained several local political leaders. The government said the changes would bring stability and end "separatism, terrorism, dynastic politics and corruption." Local journalists could not reach sources, verify information, send photographs or video, or in many cases confirm stories with editors outside the region; some had to travel to a government-run media center to use monitored internet access. Mobile and broadband internet were restored only in stages over the following months and year, and the International Federation of Journalists said journalists in Kashmir faced "declining advertising revenues, job losses, pay cuts" and "self-censorship" on top of the shutdown itself.
incidents.stated_justification: The government said the change would bring stability to the region and end "separatism, terrorism, dynastic politics and corruption"; it did not separately justify the communications shutdown beyond citing broader public-order and security concerns.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Journalists could not reach sources, verify facts, send photographs or video, or confirm stories with editors, and the International Federation of Journalists said the disruption was "an egregious violation of citizens' rights to information from a free press."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Indian government's August 2019 revocation of Article 370, which had granted Jammu and Kashmir a degree of constitutional autonomy since 1949.
incidents.outcome_note: High-speed mobile internet remained restricted into 2020; the International Federation of Journalists reported the blackout as still affecting journalists' work a full year after it began.

incidents.title: Saudi Arabia's government kills journalist Jamal Khashoggi inside its Istanbul consulate
incidents.jurisdiction: Saudi Arabia, national (extraterritorial: consulate in Istanbul, Turkey)
incidents.summary: Jamal Khashoggi, a Washington Post columnist and critic of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, was killed by Saudi agents inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul; the CIA concluded the crown prince ordered the killing, which Saudi Arabia denied.
incidents.what_happened: Jamal Khashoggi, a Saudi journalist who wrote columns for The Washington Post critical of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, entered the Saudi consulate in Istanbul, Turkey, on October 2, 2018, to obtain paperwork for his upcoming marriage, and did not come out. After more than two weeks of denials, Saudi Arabia acknowledged he had died inside the consulate, saying a team of 15 Saudi nationals sent to persuade him to return to the kingdom had killed him accidentally in a struggle; Turkish officials said the killing was planned and that his body was dismembered and never recovered. The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) concluded, based partly on intercepted communications, that the killing "would not and could not have happened" without the crown prince's approval; a Saudi government spokesperson called the assessment "false." A Saudi court later convicted eight unnamed operatives, sentencing five to death, later commuted after payments to Khashoggi's family, while clearing senior officials of responsibility.
incidents.stated_justification: Saudi officials said a 15-member team was sent only to persuade Khashoggi to return to the kingdom and that he died accidentally during a physical struggle; a Saudi spokesperson called the CIA's contrary assessment "false."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist critical of the crown prince was killed inside his own country's consulate; the CIA's assessment that the killing could not have happened without the crown prince's approval drew international scrutiny of Saudi treatment of dissenting journalists abroad.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Jamal Khashoggi's Washington Post columns criticizing Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's consolidation of power and human-rights record.
incidents.outcome_note: A Saudi court convicted eight unnamed operatives and sentenced five to death, later commuted; the CIA's assessment that the crown prince ordered the killing did not result in charges against him.

incidents.title: Venezuela expels or denies entry to dozens of foreign journalists covering anti-government protests
incidents.summary: During 2016 to 2018 protests against President Nicolas Maduro's government, Venezuelan authorities expelled, deported or denied entry to dozens of foreign correspondents, most citing bureaucratic pretexts such as visa irregularities rather than a stated substantive reason.
incidents.what_happened: As protests against President Nicolas Maduro's government intensified from 2016 into 2018, Venezuelan immigration and intelligence agencies expelled, deported or refused entry to dozens of foreign correspondents. On September 1, 2017, during a major opposition demonstration, authorities expelled five Al Jazeera English journalists, including Teresa Bo and John Holman, along with reporters for Le Monde, Colombia's Caracol, NPR and the Miami Herald. Brazilian television reporter Leandro Stoliar, detained for ten hours in 2016 while investigating a corruption case, said, "I felt like a prisoner, like a criminal." Authorities gave varied, often bureaucratic reasons, citing visa irregularities, missing equipment paperwork or unspecified immigration violations, rather than a single stated policy. Reporters Without Borders' Emmanuel Colombie said the pattern of inconsistent reasons "creates [a] climate of uncertainty and constitutes [a] threat to freedom of information." The expulsions continued into 2018 and 2019, affecting journalists from France, Spain, Peru, Argentina and elsewhere.
incidents.stated_justification: Authorities cited varied administrative reasons in different cases, including visa irregularities, missing equipment paperwork and unspecified immigration violations, rather than a single stated policy for expelling foreign correspondents.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Dozens of foreign correspondents were expelled, deported or refused entry over roughly two years; RSF's Emmanuel Colombie said the inconsistency of the reasons given "creates [a] climate of uncertainty and constitutes [a] threat to freedom of information."
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Sustained anti-government street protests in Venezuela in 2016 and 2017 over the economic crisis and President Maduro's moves to consolidate power.
incidents.outcome_note: The pattern of expulsions and entry denials continued into 2018 and 2019 with no announced change in policy in the sources reviewed.

incidents.title: Australian Federal Police raid the national broadcaster over reporting on alleged war crimes in Afghanistan
incidents.summary: Australian Federal Police spent hours searching the headquarters of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) over its 2017 "Afghan Files" reports on alleged killings by Australian special forces that breached the laws of armed conflict, seizing files under a warrant citing the Crimes Act's ban on publishing classified material.
incidents.what_happened: In 2017, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), the national public broadcaster, published the "Afghan Files," reports based on leaked defense documents describing allegations that Australian special forces killed people in breach of the laws of armed conflict. On June 5, 2019, Australian Federal Police (AFP) officers spent about eight hours searching ABC's Sydney headquarters, examining thousands of files and journalist Dan Oakes' emails, under a warrant citing the Crimes Act 1914's ban on "publishing classified material." Officers left with two USB drives of sealed files pending legal review. ABC managing director David Anderson said, "The ABC stands by its journalists, will protect its sources and continue to report without fear or favour on national security and intelligence issues when there is a clear public interest," and news director Gaven Morris said, "journalism is not a crime." The AFP said its actions were "independent and impartial at all times." The raid followed a separate police search, one day earlier, of a News Corp journalist's home over unrelated leaked material.
incidents.stated_justification: The AFP said the raid concerned "allegations of publishing classified material, contrary to provisions of the Crimes Act 1914," and separately said its investigative actions had been "independent and impartial at all times."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Police searched the newsroom for eight hours and reviewed a journalist's personal emails and thousands of files before leaving with sealed material; ABC's news director said, "journalism is not a crime," and its editorial director called the reporting "outstanding" and in the public interest.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: ABC's 2017 "Afghan Files" reporting on allegations that Australian special forces soldiers killed people in breach of the laws of armed conflict.
incidents.outcome_note: The Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions decided in October 2020 not to charge journalist Dan Oakes over the Afghan Files reporting.

incidents.title: United Kingdom detains journalist's partner under terrorism law and oversees destruction of Guardian hard drives holding Snowden files
incidents.summary: British authorities detained David Miranda, partner of Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, for nine hours at Heathrow Airport under anti-terrorism powers, and separately had Guardian staff destroy hard drives holding files leaked by Edward Snowden rather than hand them to a court.
incidents.what_happened: In August 2013, as The Guardian was reporting on National Security Agency (NSA) surveillance based on documents leaked by former contractor Edward Snowden, British authorities detained David Miranda, the partner of Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, for nine hours at London's Heathrow Airport, the maximum allowed without charge under Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000, a law letting officers stop and question travellers at ports without suspicion of a crime. Officers questioned him and seized electronic devices; the government said police were right to stop people suspected of possessing "highly sensitive stolen information that would help terrorism." Separately, British intelligence officials visited The Guardian's London offices and, editor Alan Rusbridger said, watched as Guardian staff used power drills to destroy hard drives containing Snowden material in the building's basement, after officials told the paper, in Rusbridger's account, "You've had your fun. Now we want the stuff back." Rusbridger said the paper chose destruction over handing material to a court because copies existed elsewhere, including in the United States.
incidents.stated_justification: The government said Miranda's detention was justified because he was suspected of carrying "highly sensitive stolen information that would help terrorism," and that authorities had "a duty to protect the public and our national security."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: A journalist's partner was held for nine hours and had devices seized without being charged with any offense, and Guardian staff destroyed computer hard drives under official observation rather than hand Snowden material to a court, an episode Greenwald said would only make him "far more aggressive" in reporting.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The Guardian's 2013 reporting, based on files leaked by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden, on mass surveillance by the United States and United Kingdom.
incidents.outcome_note: The Court of Appeal ruled in January 2016 that Miranda's detention itself was lawful, but found Schedule 7's stop powers incompatible with press-freedom protections for journalistic material generally.

incidents.title: Serbia's Public Information Act lets courts fine independent newspapers into financial danger
incidents.summary: Serbia's parliament passed a Public Information Act allowing courts to levy same-day fines against newspapers for vaguely defined offenses against the state's interests, and independent papers were fined far more often and more heavily than pro-government ones.
incidents.what_happened: In October 1998, Serbia's parliament, dominated by allies of Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic, passed the Law on Public Information, requiring media to avoid publishing material judged to violate "the inviolability of human dignity and the right to a private life" and barring "untruths which violate the rights of the individual," with courts empowered to impose large fines within 24 hours of a complaint and little opportunity to appeal before payment came due. By early 2000, independent outlets had received 31 fines averaging 420,000 dinars each, roughly three times the average fine on pro-government papers. Newspapers including Glas javnosti, Danas, Cacanski Glas and the magazine Vranjske were fined repeatedly. Milosevic said enforcement of the law had been "very weak" and that critics were "under foreign control"; the ruling Yugoslav Left party called for "decontamination of the journalistic profession," describing independent media as a "fifth column." The law was suspended after Milosevic lost power in October 2000.
incidents.stated_justification: President Milosevic said the law's enforcement had been "very weak" and dismissed critics as being "under foreign control"; the allied Yugoslav Left party called independent outlets a "fifth column" and demanded "decontamination of the journalistic profession."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Independent newspapers received fines nearly three times larger, on average, than pro-government papers, payable within days of a court decision, financial pressure some outlets said threatened their survival.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Independent Serbian media's coverage of NATO's escalating confrontation with Yugoslavia over Kosovo through 1998 and 1999.
incidents.outcome_note: The law was suspended after Milosevic lost power in October 2000 elections and a change of government in Serbia.
